601.t: Where Globe Hall stood and what it looked like
601.s: Russell asks where the Globe Hall was. Tom and Martin place it near Congress Square beside the basin, a tall upstairs hall entered from Crown Letters Wall with a bandstand six or seven feet high, like Economy Hall.
601.q: He used to sit there in the square. And see? Right in the next street. Yeah, right there. You see the back of it was on St. Peter. And the front of it was on Crown Letters Wall.

601.t: Economy Hall, Hope Hall and bandstands in the old halls
601.s: They compare the balcony and bandstand in other old halls and the church Economy Hall. Hope Hall, whose front blew in during a hurricane, is due to be torn down, and they describe its high rear bandstand.
601.q: Right in the back. Yeah. You go all the way back and in the back they had the steps going down on both sides. Both sides. Each side. And between the steps they had a bandstand that was high. Yeah.

601.t: Old halls still standing across the river: Eureka Hall
601.s: Russell asks which old Algiers halls survive so he can photograph them. Martin names Eureka Hall at the Cut-Off and mentions two or three small halls and a school.
601.ch: Algiers places, ball games and Frankie Duson
601.q: That's me. Eureka. I'm talking about them old halls. Yeah, because I know Bob played back in the school there back there. He played at the school. Yeah. The school that's built there. The school that's built there. I'm speaking about when the halls was down there when Charlie McDowell and them was…

601.t: Halls and bands of the period: Morets, Imperial, Hope Hall, Globe Hall, Funky Butt
601.s: Martin runs through the halls and the bands tied to them: old man Moret, Manuel Perez's Imperial, Freddie Keppard, Hope Hall, the Globe Hall by the basin, and the Funky Butt Hall on Perdido Street.
601.ch: Jimmy Noon, Nene Quacku and the barbers
601.q: Now you take, you take pretty much all them halls that that time they had, they band. You take the Franz Ami, that was old man Morett in them. Yeah. Old man Morett. Yeah, Morett, yeah. He was a carnet player. That's right. That's right. Old man Morett. You know, you take, you take, of course, you…

601.t: The Flying Mexican Hall in Algiers, 1905
601.s: Martin says he first heard the band at the Flying Mexican Hall in Jules's Lane in 1905 with Tom Albert. He describes the wooden hall, its location near George Lewis's house and its Saturday-night dances.
601.ch: Algiers halls and the picnic boat
601.q: That's right. That's the Flying Mexican Hall. Down in Jules's Lane. Was that Algiers? That's Algiers. Over in Algiers. Jules's Lane.

241.t: School concerts, fraternity and law school parties, and a far-back dance hall
241.s: Concerts and parties for students and a dance in McDonoughville, then returning to Larry and the changes of ownership to Mills and Jaffe.
241.q: Then after that we played several parts. We played for the ball game. The fellas of this boy had a ball club, you know? Oh, that was a fraternity. I think that was a K fraternity.

241.t: Playing at a hall on Napoleon and Tchoupitoulas; Tin Roof
241.s: They played Wednesday, Friday and Sunday at a hall near Napoleon and Tchoupitoulas whose name neither can recall; Russell asks about Albert Burbank and the Tin Roof.
241.q: I forgot what the name of that thing, I forgot what the name of that place. It's right on the corner of Lopold in, what's it called, the street, Charter. Not Charter or.

241.t: Other dance halls he played on the west bank
241.s: Russell asks about other halls; Valentine lists country clubs and halls he played for, and they agree there were many on that side of the river.
241.q: Well I played, Mr. Bill, look I played, I played at Al J's Country Club way down low cove way in the back. Oh yeah. I played, I used to play for a fella by the river here, right by the river. I used to play for a fella, he had a dance hall. I played for him, Mr. Watney, he had a dance hall. I…

248.t: Tin Top Hall, Kenny's Hall (Funky Butt) and Perdido Street halls
248.s: Dawson identifies Tin Top as a small hall on Perdido with a tin roof, nearby Kenny's Hall called the Funky Butt, and the Zulu Club.
248.q: That was on Pedida. Pedida between, uh, between, uh, Franklin and Liberty Franklin. Tintop. Tintop. On the left hand side. Small hall, eh? Still in? Oh, no, that thing is gone. Oh, yeah.

248.t: Billy Phillips' dance hall and George Jones
248.s: Description of the Tuxedo/Billy Phillips hall on Franklin Street and Phillips' place uptown run by George Jones.
248.ch: Billy Phillips, George Jones and the Shriners trip
248.q: Place? Billy Phillips. Billy Phillips. Billy Phillips on, on, on, that was on, on Franklin. Yeah, between Ivville and Bimble on the left-hand side. Yeah. Yeah, he had a place there, too, yeah. But he didn't have much of a dancing place there, you know. Like a hall and a ball. And they had two…

248.t: Hall layouts and playing at the Pelican with Kid Rene
248.s: Bandstand versus balcony halls; Dawson and Kid Rene played the Pelican, starting on the front gallery.
248.q: No, no. Oh, that was the Pelican, like, was on Rampard and Gravia. That was, that had a stairs that go up. Balcony in front. Yeah. That's where we, uh, me and Kid Rene was playing it. We played there. I played there with Rene at the Pelican. On Rampard between, uh, Neb Gravia. Yes, I know by Neb…

246.t: Society halls: Columny, Poise de Viernes, and Big Eye Louis's home
246.s: Glass talks of the old society halls he belonged to, what became of them, and visits to clarinettist Big Eye Louis Nelson.
246.ch: Bands, halls and the Smoky Mary
246.q: That ain't the district. No, it was Irsaline. I was down in the Oisaline. We had the Poise of Viernes Hall. We had the Frasier Me Hall. But they're still there now. Yeah, they're still there. The Poise of Viernes Hall. The church now, they made a church at the Poise of Viernes. Well that's nice.…

246.t: The Plum Plan hall, later the American Legion hall
246.s: Talk about the Plum Plan dance hall, its name, its remodeling into the American Legion hall, and its location.
246.ch: Bands, lake camps and early players
246.q: Yeah. It's a funny name. Plum Plan? Plum Plan. It used to call it. Oh. Then the American Legion moved, they moved back to Franklin Avenue on that.

246.t: Playing dance halls and the back-room saloon dancing
246.s: Glass recalls playing in a few places, including a back-room saloon run by Papa, and the interviewers ask about the district's dance halls.
246.ch: Bands, halls and the Smoky Mary
246.q: Old fella, they used to call him Papa, I believe. He had some daughters, Papa.

1000.t: The old halls now turned churches: Perseverance and others
1000.s: They identify Perseverance Hall, Economy Hall and other dance halls that are now churches.
1000.q: That's the Hall right there, it's a church now, it's a church now right there. That's the Copper Raiders Hall, that's the, I mean the Perseverance Hall. Perseverance, that's it right there.

1000.t: Halls where he played: Celestan, Piku, St. Teresa Hall and others
1000.s: He played banquets at a hall with George Astute and Joe Nicholas, worked once with Celestan at St. Teresa Hall, and gave his own dance with Rena.
1000.q: And Dave, Dave, what do you mean? Dave, that's all I know used to play. And Chani, used to play with Chani. I had a job at the last roundup, used to play with Chani and Po Re. I played so many different places at the last roundup, yeah, we used to play there, me and Chani and he's living here,…

1000.t: High bandstands in the old halls
1000.s: Discussion of halls with raised bandstands, Nunciation Street club, Artesian, Economy, Perseverance and Francs Amis halls.
1000.q: Yeah, the bandstand was up high. People used to dance down. The cabaret was on the first floor. The cabaret was on the first floor. The bandstand was up looking down on the floor. Yeah. They got that carnival, that club uptown got the bandstand like that. Cause I played up there a couple of years…

174.t: The Pythian Temple roof garden with multiple bands
174.s: The Pythian Temple stage and balconies held four or five bands on Monday nights.
174.q: Oh yeah well they had a stage and sometimes they sit two bands on that stage, sometimes one. And they had a balcony all around you see.

174.t: Playing the Bienville Roof Sunday dances
174.s: Dejan recalls Sunday evening dances on the Bienville Hotel roof in the 1920s, and a furniture-store owner who hired the band.
174.q: The Bienville Hotel. I think Stanley was playing piano. It was Billy's sister if I'm not mistaken, Bill Phillips and my brother and myself and Ruben McClendon was playing a banjo. We'll get him one night. I don't know where he lived. But he was playing banjo and he could play piano pretty good too.…

957.t: The Masonic hall on Dolphin Street and other dance halls
957.s: Russell and Foster sort out a hall on Dolphin Street, once white and now Black, versus one at Mandeville and Rampart.
957.q: Yeah. Mr. Wakes can tell you about that. Johnny Wakes. Yes, he told us about it. Yeah. Yeah, that's probably good. So we should do that more.

957.t: The old schoolhouse hall at Touro and Dolphin; halls burned and rebuilt
957.s: A former schoolhouse with dancing downstairs burned twice and was rebuilt; Foster first played the Mandeville and Rampart hall with Chris Kelly, and a white hall is mentioned.
957.q: You say they used to have the school upstairs, and they danced downstairs. Oh, yeah. The hall downstairs. And that's the Turo and Dolphin. Turo and Dolphin, yeah.

869.t: Dance halls: Globe, Funky Butt, Economy Hall, Masonic Hall
869.s: Adams lists halls where he danced, on Camp, Eagle, near Basin Street and North Line, as he and the interviewers sort out locations.
869.q: The other ones were down on Camp Street. It was right there between Valance and up in there. And then the other one, the Funky Butt Hall was down there. Back around near Basin Street, called the Funky Butt Hall. And they had a hall they called the Economy Hall, but I just remember where the Economy…

869.t: Adams the dancer, not a musician; Love and Charity Hall
869.s: Interviewer notes Adams never played an instrument but heard bands and danced; he places the Love and Charity Hall uptown.
869.q: Now, I danced a lot. I used to go to the hall they called the Love and Charity Hall. Where was that, do you remember? The Love and Charity Hall was on camp, I think, right between Valance and some way up in Alabama.

681.t: Dance halls around Elysian Fields and the Hollywood
681.s: Third Ward dance halls, the open-air Hollywood owned by Sharkey and Leon Prima, Dave Winstein and Nina Pecone, and Al Rose's book.
681.q: That was, there was, well, you see, there was a lot of people down around that neighborhood. I mean, Uptown was, was a different class of people. It was a, uppity people. But, uh, around that third ward, they, they enjoyed their lives. They enjoyed dancing and things like that. It was, it was more,…

681.t: Locating the Elysian Fields dance halls and Pete Fountain's place
681.s: They try to place the dance hall; upstairs halls with galleries, and Pete's club on Royal Street, are discussed.
681.q: It was probably Burgundy Street. It wasn't where Pete was. Pete was on Royal. He was at Lusitannis, huh? He was on Royal Street.

290.t: The Music Box jitney dance at Carondelet and Canal
290.s: He worked a couple of weeks at the Music Box, a continuous jitney dance, replacing Arnold Metoyer.
290.ch: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
290.q: Yeah, I worked there a couple of weeks, it got too tough for me, because you had to continue, play continuously, you couldn't stop. You know, the, yeah, just like when I go to the sort of a Jitney style stuff. You paid for a dance and you couldn't stop, you'd take no rest. In other words, the way…

290.t: Manuel Ridgley and the Pelican dance hall
290.s: He played upstairs at the Pelican, run by Manuel Ridgley, with the Silver Leaf and Nola bands; Royal Garden and Astoria nearby.
290.ch: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
290.q: His brother was, Will Ridley was a trombone player. Manuel Ridley was running a business for Farbacher at Rand Fortin Common. You played that there? Yeah, I played up there on the sort of a dance hall upstairs. Oh yeah? Over there. I played there quite often.

855.t: How he found the musicians in New Orleans
855.s: He went to Preservation Hall and Dixieland Hall and got an address from Mrs. Jaffe.

855.t: Comparing New Orleans venues and sign-off
855.s: He compares Preservation Hall, Dixieland Hall and the Old Absinthe House; the recording ends.
855.q: Also, I myself was only in three places. That was Preservation Hall, Dixieland Hall and Absinthe House. I was not in the paddock, because it was for me first to expensive. And since you can hear the music from outside and I also know who plays, I just hold for the cappella just for the trumpet. I…

637.t: King's Hall, Funky Butt Hall and Kennie's Hall
637.s: Bolden at King's Hall (Funky Butt), Kennie's Hall and its owner, and a clown named George.
637.q: Well, uh, they had, uh, that's why I used to see Bowling most of the time. Out on, on Padilla Street, he used to play there, the King's Hall. King's Hall. King's Hall. He used to. Oh yes, Kennies.

637.s: Balconied halls, Economy and Hope Hall, and other halls he played, most of them downtown.
637.q: The cooperators got two on each other. Well, the cooperators, that hall is still here, I believe somebody. Yeah, yeah, they got a church out there.

296.t: Dance halls: Mississippi Valley, Globe and Lek-E-Tay
296.s: He recalls playing for dances and Mardi Gras balls at several halls.
296.q: I used to play. Yeah, that's what St. Peter's was St. Globes. That's right. That's right.

296.t: Economy Hall, Globe Hall and playing in the balcony
296.s: Economy Hall and Globe Hall balls; musicians played in the balcony.
296.q: You know, the lawn showman's all burned just before Christmas.

1.t: New Orleans halls, clubs and who played for each social level
1.s: Barker lists clubs such as the Bulls and Bears and trumpeters like Perez, Oliver, Rena and Petit, each serving a different social stratum.
1.ch: Second session: family, Armstrong and David Jones
1.q: That’s where he had a nest, a boomerang, I’d say, to bust out. They were young then, and they were all experimenting. They had all these halls, which you don’t have in them other towns. You had 15 to 20 black halls, and that’s not counting the clubs. The Lions Club, the Bulls Club, the Saints and…

1.t: The downtown halls and clubs, one for every color
1.s: Danny lists Economy Hall, Cooperators Hall, Globe Hall, San Jacinto and the Lions Club, each for a different color stratum.
1.ch: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
1.q: On Liberty and Marais. Two blocks from that, at Lafitte and Orleans, was the Globe Hall, which ceased to be a hall, and became a gambling house. Then you had the First Veterans Hall. Then you had... All these halls were about four blocks from one another. I'll show you where they were. And then…

173.t: Dance halls and rifle clubs: Thoman's Hall, Rifle Club, Unexpected Rifle Club
173.s: Locations of halls where he played dances, including volunteer rifle clubs with good floors.
173.q: The wigwam, wasn't it? Huh? The wigwam, wasn't it? Yeah, I mean, so, it was Thoman's Hall. Thoman's Hall was on the lakeside of Dauphin Street. Uh-huh.

175.s: They list closed or converted halls: Cooperators, San Jacinto, Lions, Frontiers, Economy, Perseverance, Autocrat.
175.q: There used to be no, every little corner of the band. No, there's nobody in the neighborhood. Not now. The Cooperators Hall is gone, the San Jacincense is gone, the Lions is gone, the Bowles is gone, the Bowles Club is gone, the Frons Amis is gone. Well of course I guess they used that Frons Amis…

245.s: He lists the halls he played in New Orleans.
245.q: Boy, yeah, I played in the Economy Hall. I played in the Santa Sena Club. I played in the Bulls Club. And I played in the Hopes Hall. Sacred Hall of Mary's in the Algea's? Yeah, I played in the Sacred Hall in the Algea's. And it's a hall uptown I used to play on. St. Elizabeth? I played in St.…

567.t: The halls and societies he knew
567.s: White names the halls he frequented, including St. Dominic, Economy Hall and others, and the clubs and societies he followed.
567.q: I wouldn't been to the Connemy Hall, the San Sioux Hall, you know where the San Sioux Hall is there? The St. Dominic. I don't know where that's at. That's up in Coctin. That's up on the bridge between Genet and Hickory. But it's mostly locally on the riverside. That's where it's at. I done been to…

457.t: Dance music and halls in New Orleans
457.s: He played with Fields and Planchet for club dances, at halls like Francs Amis.
457.q: Yes, because I played... I played with a... Even while I was studying classic side, I played with an orchestra there named Fields and Planchet. And that was the popular combination for most of the club dancers. And I did quite a bit of playing with them.

181.t: America's Hall, Geddes Hall and Planters Hotel
181.s: Parker does not know the halls named.
181.q: I heard of it, but I never heard of it.

899.s: He names Economy Hall, other society halls, the Tulane Club and a merry-go-round job, used for dances, banquets and weddings.
899.q: Well, I played at the Economy Hall, I played at the Poiseuilers Hall, at the New Hall, at the Hopes Hall.

254.t: Bizat Park, McGuire's, the Love and Charity Hall and Carrollton
254.s: They discuss baseball at Bizat Park, a gambling club, Southport, the Love and Charity Hall uptown and music along Carrollton.
254.q: You know, that's where the club was, that club is what I used to be.

921.s: Father played jitney or taxi dances on Canal Street; Harold recalls his own band at the job he got from James Davis, and playing with P. Roy and Walter P. Sean.
921.q: He used to play on Canal Street. Yeah. Canal between Villery and.

257.t: Rehearsals near his house and a hall near the Union
257.s: Bands including Sonny South's rehearsed across from his house, and musicians played Saturday dances at a hall near the Musicians' Union, possibly called the Nile Hall.
257.ch: Neighborhood halls and the Ida Cox tour
257.q: Well, they used to rehearse across the street from my house. Now, my other brother, one he still plays. He works with Larry every now and then. They used to rehearse about my house. Gene Ware, they used to jam. You know Gene Ware, Harold DeJong, quite a few fellas. Earl Bostic and all of them had…

710.t: Uptown dance halls, downtown bands and color lines at halls
710.s: Bailey went to the Winter Garden and Rube Garden, recalls where the old downtown musicians played, and says he was too dark for some halls.
710.q: Well, yeah, I used to go to dances, yeah. I used to go to that Rube Garden. Oh yeah. I used to go to another place on Grabby Street. The way we used to do, we wouldn't have no kind of money to go in the dead. We'd send one fella with my hat. We asked the man to let him take, go see for my hat. The…

969.t: Places where society dances were held
969.s: Audubon Tea Room, Tulane Gym, the Quartier Club, the Sazerac Bar and fraternity dances, as distinct from cabarets; interviewer mentions a rough club behind chicken wire.
969.ch: New Orleans dance scene of the 1920s
969.q: And so, you might be interested in knowing some of the places that these dances were given, in addition to private homes, of course. Or places like the Audubon Tea Room, Tulane Gym, the Cartier Club. Have you heard of it? Never have.

14.t: The band at the dance house across Bayou Rapides
14.s: A band of Pensacola Kid, Clarence Williams, Bunk Johnson and Baby Lovett works at a dance-hall house with girls across the bayou.
14.q: Uh huh. Like a little island over there. Uh huh. Nothing but fast. Help people. I got the picture. Of it now. And that's where Bunk, Dineswil, Paul Wilde, David Luggan.

266.t: Ballrooms and supper clubs in New Orleans
266.s: They agree New Orleans never had a big Roseland-type ballroom, discussing the Fern, hotel ballrooms, the Blue Room and the Jung roof.
266.ch: New Orleans ballrooms and Tony Almerico
266.q: I don't remember either, but then that would, see that would be like slightly before my time. Yeah. When ballrooms were popular. Yeah. I can remember Eddie Miller talking about the Fern Dance Hall. Yeah. And a couple more places if the names don't come to mind right now. And I imagine that maybe…

995.t: Engagements, Ralph Foster and Mike DeLay at the Lavida dance hall
995.s: Lists hotel and boat engagements around 1927, then playing with Ralph Foster and Mike DeLay at the Lavida on Iberville until 1934, describing the hall and its bandstand.
995.q: Around 26, I believe, from about around 27. So, all the doing that, that next year is when I went to a dance hall. We had so many engagements during them years, back in 27. We played our chair by Jack Sheen. We played on the boat, the captain. We played at the Junk Hotel. We played at the Rosecrunk…

269.t: Creole dance halls of downtown New Orleans
269.s: She lists halls such as L'Amitie, Perseverance, Artisans, L'Equite and Sincere, and locates them.
269.q: Oh, yes. They had L'Amitié. They had Perseverance. They had Artisans. How do they call that little hall on Robinson Street? L'Equite. L'Equite.

187.t: Not playing the Storyville-district dance halls
187.s: He did not play the 101 Ranch or Pete Lala's but visited, and remembers Mr. Pena on drums.
187.q: See, they had their own band there. All I can remember was, when Mr. Pena, he used to play drums and I didn't pay too much to the other people who was playing there. I used to go there every night and we'd knock off it, sit and stop by there, see what was going on.

403.t: Halls and parks where Bolden played
403.s: Jones names Masonic Hall, Valley Hall, Jackson Street Hall, St. Elizabeth Hall, Lincoln Park, Johnson Park and Providence Hall, and tells of Bolden calling his children home from Johnson Park.
403.q: Well, the Masonic Hall, and the, uh, the place is, it's broke up now. The Valley Hall? The Valley? The Valley Hall used to be on Party Street. It used to be on Party Street.

628.t: Weddings and the halls where he played
628.s: Williams recalls the many weddings he played and tries to name the halls, including a white club off Airline Highway.
628.q: I swamped a wedding, man. Italian Hall, First of Regents, Demolage, I mean that's under Betsy. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. It's Hall here by the Picayune office, the name of it. Uh-huh. That hall up there by the Picayune office. Uh-huh.

972.s: Asked about uptown dances, he names halls and a Perdido Street dance, saying uptown bands played mostly blues.
972.q: I've been all to Masonic, Globesaw, and New Hall and all them places, downtown, I've been all over. I wonder if you ever went uptown and heard the dances up there too, danced up there. Yeah, like there's a place called, what used to call, it's been on Frankie Street. On Frankie Street, on Frankie…

1008.t: Dance halls across the river: Casinos, Elks, Eagle Eye Hall
1008.s: Russell asks about halls in Algiers and Gretna; Morgan recalls clubs there and the Eagle Eye Hall.
1008.q: Do you remember any other clubs over in there? Well all the clubs that I knew over there was the Elks and I knew the Young Men's of Algea, the Young Men's of McDonaville and they have the Wolf.

630.t: Winter Garden, Royal Garden and the temple roof garden
630.s: They sort out the downtown halls, the Winter Garden, Pelican and Knights of Pythias temple roof garden.
630.q: No, see, Farbacker was on the Pelican, used to own the Winter Garden too, where they called it the Royal Garden when they got ready. But the original name was the Royal Garden, they called it the Winter Garden. Because it was a good place to go in the winter. See, the temple used to be closed in…

631.t: The district, halfway house, Bucktown and Bruning's
631.s: Subbing in the district and at Bucktown dance places, Bruning's Pavilion.
631.ch: Brown's Band in Chicago and New York
631.q: fights that started around there all the time. Well, there used to be Bruning's Pavilion. Yeah. The Brunings were the sheriffs out there. Anybody started a fight got beat up and put in jail. They broke the fighting up pretty quickly. That's Bruning, not Brunus. Bruning. No, not Brunus. Bruning.…

664.t: Bill Walde's family and a benefit at the Plum Plan
664.s: He names the Walde brothers and recalls a benefit dance at the low tin-roofed Plum Plan.
664.ch: Back to the horn: house sessions
664.q: dear playing clarinet and I can't recall the piano man. And I can't recall the bass man.

188.s: They discuss St. Dominic Hall, Eagle Hall, and the social aid clubs that still parade.
188.q: near Protection Levy. Is that still in Carleton? Yes, sir. That was still in Carleton. That was about a block from Protection Levy. Protection Levy, right on the other side of Protection there was Jefferson Tarish. Oh, yes.

632.t: Neighborhood bars that doubled as dance halls
632.s: They compare places like Lutton's with a bar in front and hall behind, their acoustics, and similar spots in Algiers and Marrero.
632.q: No, it wouldn't have been. You know, the inside was fairly, was pretty much square or rectangular and didn't have much built in around. Some of them had pretty good acoustics, some of them didn't. I think the main thing people wanted was for the bands to play fairly loud, and that was fun. We went…

282.t: Early jobs and dance halls with Sam Morgan
282.s: He lists halls played weekend nights, including Economy Hall on Mondays and the Saint Sue Hall on Howard, and talks about their present state.
282.q: That was up, up in the Gordon District. Or uptown. Mm-hmm. We used to play up, up there on a Saturday night, and play at Estore. Yeah, the hotel over on the drive-the-Range. Yeah. Played there on a Sunday night. Well, we had Saturday night, Sunday night, Monday night. That's about three to a week.

819.t: The Owl Club, dance halls and the few trombonists who played for Giardina
819.s: Places played in those days and the two trombonists, Edwards and Henry Brunies, who could play for Giardina.
819.q: It didn't register with me, you know. Yeah. The places we played in those days was the Lusitania, which is still on Leach and Field and Dauphine, I think. Yeah. And the Taunty Dancing School, which is out of existence for many years. And Millenburg, and I suppose. Who was out there

777.t: Dance halls at Elysian Fields and Charters
777.s: Williams describes a dance hall on the river side and the four-piece band he played with there twice.
777.ch: Routine bands and the lake dances
777.q: I don't know that fella's name. Brownskins fella playing piano. Earl Williams. I don't know. He might be. He might be the right band. Kid Milton? That's not him.

570.t: Miracle Hall, San Jacinto Hall and other venues
570.s: Discussion of halls where Penn played with Rena and Buddy Petit, and venues he never played.
570.ch: Buddy Petit's death, Milneburg and halls
570.q: Years back we used to play at the San Suu, you know, you remember the San Suu Hall? Yeah. How about that? Well we played there many times too, Randy and Buddy P.T. played the heavy bands there all the time. That's old time, that's a long time ago you know. That hall's still there.

404.t: Layout of the hall and club banquets
404.s: Dance hall downstairs, members' offices and card room upstairs; Mitchell fixed a lounge, and clubs held banquets there.
404.q: And on the second floor was the members, all the members, they had an office and different things. I was in that room where they played cards there.

779.t: Hal Jordy, Stratakos and the Musicians Ball
779.s: Where he heard Hal Jordy, vibes player, Emil Tasso in the union book, balls.
779.ch: Stories of players and the sister
779.q: I heard, I'll tell you where I think I heard Hal Geordie, let's see. I heard Hal Geordie when he was playing in a place on Canal Street. I thought he had Von Gammann who was playing drums, but I might be wrong about that. It could have been this guy that lives along the Gulf Coast, might have been…

287.t: Hall conditions: balcony bandstands, no floor shows, few singers
287.s: Halls offered straight bands with no floor shows, seldom a piano, and the band on a balcony. Morand recalls being allowed to sit up with his heroes. Musicians rarely sat in and only the trumpeter sang, if anyone.
287.ch: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
287.q: Just had a straight band? Yeah just straight band. Very few halls had a piano even. Because we used to play up in a sort of a balcony in the halls. About ten feet from the floor. And that would keep the musicians free, people crowding around. And in my young days I knew quite a few musicians and…

288.t: Dance halls compared for sound; Economy Hall and Francs Amis
288.s: Charles says Economy Hall was easiest to play; Francs Amis had a high ceiling that wore out the lip.
288.ch: Maple Leaf, own orchestra and rivals
288.q: The ceiling was too high, you see? And you could just blow your brains out, you didn't get anything out of it.

405.t: Is Preservation Hall the home of New Orleans jazz
405.s: They discuss whether the Hall is the best regular place to hear authentic New Orleans dance band music compared with Dixieland Hall and private parties.
405.q: I'm not talking about street bands. Well, I mean, I'm talking about, in, in dance bands now. I'm not talking about street bands. Well, I think people's homes, you have to consider that, private parties. Yeah, yeah.

176.s: Ernest lists dance halls such as Artesian Hall and Economy Hall.
176.q: He played there. He played too. Yeah. The Yorval Room.

127.t: St. Elizabeth Hall and lawn parties
127.s: Questions about particular halls and lawn parties, including a yard where Armstrong sat in.
127.ch: New Orleans halls and street bands
127.q: Yeah, sure. That's the hall I tried to call. That's up above the Poirier Avenue. That's the one I tried to call, St. Elizabeth.

884.t: Algiers society halls and dance pavilions
884.s: Russell asks about halls: the Young Men's hall, a former open pavilion owned by Friends of Progress, and the Odd Fellows halls.
884.q: Yeah, one down here, and then they have another young man up here. Oh, that's okay. That's the hall. Yeah, the young men's hall. That's still there. That's still there. Yeah. Well that's, the bands that, right now, well that's gone now. That's right the next, on the canal there. Used to be a canal…

666.t: Photo of a script dance at the Chess and Checkers Club
666.s: Rau explains the photograph taken at a script dance in the Cosmopolitan Hotel's Chess and Checkers Club on Bourbon Street, versus the formal Blue Room picture.
666.q: Well, it was an old script dance. I don't know who promoted it. We used to have two or three people that made a living out of it, that kept themselves in school by giving these script dances every once in a while. Most of them were given a two-lane gym, the old gym. But this happened to be one…

896.t: Dance halls like the San Su and what the dancing was like
896.s: Halls such as the San Su on South Street were dominated by Kelly and Carey; the dances were real dancing, with no rock and roll.
896.ch: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
896.q: Yeah. I never looked up inside. Oh, that place was in a bloom. The Saint-Sue, the Corporate Hall downtown, the Frantz Amis, all of that. Yeah. Chris had that sewed up. And when Chris wasn't there, Jack had it sewed up. That's right.

476.t: Dance halls and Blue Monday over here
476.s: They played mostly rented dance halls, with Monday the big night, though Blue Monday was never a custom as in New Orleans.
476.ch: Early bands around Bay St. Louis
476.q: Oh well they'd give, we'd play mostly at these dance halls. dance halls. You're in? Promote, yeah. Promote Vanellan Association had a hall, they'd rent, and we was playing most, we played about once a week then, every Monday. That was a big

303.t: Bourbon Street jazz revivals and the jitney dance halls
303.s: Bandstand on Bourbon Street, crowds, jazz returning every 25 years and its roots in taxi dance halls.
303.q: Louis Escobeda played trumpet and vibra harp. Ah. That was when the bandstand faced the front of Bourbon Street. You know what I'm saying? Faced Bourbon Street. We saw it completely renovated three times, enlarged on account of it. And eyeballs at that time started off at 65 cents. And many of the…

806.t: Empty bandstands, ballparks, and the Village Vanguard
806.s: He feels the same possibility looking at an empty stage or ball field, and recalls Vanguard gigs with McLean, Slide Hampton, Hargrove and McBride.
806.q: Yeah to be honest, yeah. I mean you know usually not, usually not. I always look at the bandstand or the stage you know when you look at a piano or even if there’s no piano but particularly when there’s a piano and a drumset and maybe an amp for the bass, and whatever it may be, whatever the set-up…

4.t: Mosby's Dixieland Blue Blowers at Solomon's Dance Pavilion
4.s: Solomon's on Grand Avenue held thousands daily; Henry Starr led the piano there after his first cabaret job with Spikes.
4.ch: Shows, scripts and the Mosby-era names
4.q: Oh, I think it was Grand Avenue and Twelfth--or something like that. Or Grand Avenue and Ninth, I think it was. Ninth and Tenth. That was a big dancehall there, you know, and they played there afternoon and night. They had two sessions a day, and that was a...they had just thousands of people there…
